sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: A series of frontal systems will bring a return of widespread rain and occasionally windy conditions today through the weekend. A trend toward drier and cooler conditions are expected toward the middle portion of next week as the storm track shifts south of Western Washington.

sections.title: Short term (today through Sunday)
paragraphs: Rain is spreading onto the coast this morning ahead of the first of a couple frontal systems that will impact the region in the days ahead. Along with the rain, breezy to locally windy conditions will develop along the coast, the North Interior, and near the Cascade gaps. A combination of high tide and lower atmospheric pressure will contribute to minor to moderate coastal flooding today as well. Larger seas building to around 20 feet will reach the coast where a high surf advisory remains in effect. Rain will turn to showers by tonight as an upper trough axis shifts onshore.

A second and stronger frontal system will move into the area later Saturday into Saturday night. QPF remains in the same ballpark as previous estimates with around 1.5 to 2 inches for much of the coast, 3+ inches on the south facing slopes of the Olympics, and somewhere between 0.50 and 1 inch for much of the interior lowlands. NBM probabilities of wind gusts exceeding 50 mph along portions of the coast are around 60 to 80 percent for Saturday afternoon/evening with another bullseye of 50 to 60 percent probabilities near the east entrance to the strait later Saturday night. Elsewhere, peak wind gusts Saturday night will be roughly 30 to 40 mph. Post-frontal showers continue into Sunday with winds easing.

sections.title: Long term (Sunday night through Thursday)
paragraphs: An upper trough will move into the area Sunday night and Monday and introduce a notably cooler air mass from what we've seen recently. QPF will be light by this time, but snow levels will dip to around 4000 feet. Models are continuing the trend of the next system toward the middle of next week taking a more southern track and just clipping the far southern portion of the CWA. Beyond that, upper ridging is on track to bring a period of drier weather to round out the remainder of the week. And this time of year, that probably means some fog and cool temperatures.

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: A frontal system is moving onshore as widespread rainfall spreads along the coast. This activity will continue inland as the morning progress. Ceilings will briefly dip to MVFR as the rain pushes through, but VFR is favored for much of the day. Low level wind shear may impact terminals as the frontal system moves through. Rainfall will transition to showers by this evening with a slight chance (less than 15%) chance of thunder along the coast. Mostly VFR is expected tonight into Saturday morning but can't rule out areas of MVFR as well. Surface winds will generally remain south/southeast through the period, with winds generally 5-10 kt with gusts to 20 kt for the Puget Sound terminals and higher gusts up to 30 kt along the coast.

KSEA...VFR conditions with high clouds. A frontal system will push inland between 15z-18z, bringing rain and potential for low level wind shear at the terminal. While conditions are expected to remain predominantly VFR, MVFR may briefly develop in heavier rainfall. Winds will generally remain out of the south or southeast around 10 kt or less, with gusts to 20 kt developing at the terminal later this evening. VFR conditions are favored tonight into Saturday morning.

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: SCAs will remain for the East Strait, Admiralty Inlet and Grays Harbor Bar well into tonight. A SCA has been issued for the West Strait as well for the remainder of the morning before dropping off this afternoon due to ESE winds reaching criteria. Gales gusts are firmly in place across the coastal waters as an occasional storm force gust cannot be ruled out, particularly over the outer coastal waters. SCA winds look to potentially pick up later tonight into Saturday morning for the Northern Inland waters

Winds over the inner waters will remain elevated into Saturday morning, winds over the coastal waters will briefly decrease as gales transition to more Small Craft strength. However, the next frontal system is set to arrive late Saturday afternoon as a sub 970 mb low generates very strong southerly winds. REFS probabilities are now showing greater than 90% chance of Storm Force gusts being met over the outer and inner coastal waters while the NBM is showing 50- 60% into Saturday night. Small Craft winds are favored to continue on Sunday, at least over the coastal waters and portions of the inland waters Conditions are favored to calm by Monday, with potential for continued windy conditions over the waters returning by Tuesday.

Today's system will bring very large seas to the Washington coast, with high confidence in waves building to 20-26 ft over the coastal waters by this afternoon. These large waves will also be very energetic, with a dominant period of 18 to 20 seconds. Seas will remain elevated through Saturday morning and will briefly ease a bit into early Sunday, remaining between 14 to 18 feet. Another system will send another round of large, long period waves on Sunday with another round of waves likely 20-22 ft or higher through Monday morning. Seas look to ease a bit after Monday, but will likely stay in the 12-15 foot range heading into the middle of next week.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: A series of frontal storm systems bring will bring periods of high surf and sneaker waves to the coast and rain and breezy conditions areawide through at least early next week. Snow will begin to fall above 4000 ft in the Cascades late Sunday into Monday.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Water vapor satellite imagery shows an upper level pinching and cutting off the southern California coast. Meanwhile, a deep low pressure is spinning over the northeast Pacific and shifting east-southeastward towards the Pacific Northwest. An earlier WPC surface analysis estimated the surface low pressure at 960mb.

Ensembles are in good agreement this strong low pressure will push a front towards the coast late tonight before pushing into the I-5 corridor around daybreak. A strong wind field of 60-70 kt at 925mb will develop off the southern and central coast of Oregon before the front makes landfall. East to west pressure gradient forces should keep most of these winds off the coast, particularly off the north Oregon and south Washington coast.. However, the pressure gradients do open ever so slightly that some of this wind field could be realized at our most exposed locations along the central coast of Oregon. Right now estimating there is a 30% chance that our windiest sites meet High Wind Warning criteria with lower odds north of Tillamook County. As a result, will hold off on any high wind products, but will need to monitor trends and monitor buoy observations to see how well they are tracking with modeled wind fields. Either way, given the pressure gradients the strongest winds are unlikely to last more than 1-2 hours along any portion of the coast, which should reduce impacts. The bigger impact of this storm system will be another round of high surf along the coast late Friday into early Saturday. See the beach hazards section below for more information.

Models and their ensembles are in good agreement an embedded shortwave trough will swing northeastward into the area Friday afternoon into early evening, which should aid in creating a more organized band of showers spreading into the region around that time. Cooler sea surface temperatures near the coast may limit vigorous convection coming onto the coast, but wind fields will be supportive of some rotating storms farther offshore Friday.

The next storm system is currently south of the Aleutian Islands and will shift eastward over the next 48 hours. As it does so, another low pressure will deepen rapidly to around 960mb and move into the place of the current existing low pressure over the northeast Pacific. This will push another front eastward into the region Saturday night bringing another round of increased winds along the coast. It appears there is a 30% chance for a low end High Wind event along the coast late Saturday before a cooler and more showery weather regime takes hold. Snow levels will drop from above 6000 ft early Sunday to near 4000 ft by Monday morning. Given unmaintained mountain roads are free of snow and open, will likely need a Winter Weather product for the Cascades even if only a few inches of snow fall Sunday night into Monday.
There looks to be a brief lull in the wet and breezy weather Tuesday-ish before most global ensemble members suggest another storm system impacts the region around Wednesday of next week. /Neuman

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 06Z Saturday...Upper level cloud are streaming in ahead of an approaching cold front that will impact the region later tonight. Breaks in the cloud cover have allowed for some patchy fog to develop in the typical foggy spots around the Willamette Valley. Expecting conditions to marginally improve as the front moves east, increasing winds but also bringing light to moderate rain. Chances for rain increase at the coast after 08z, spreading inland by 11-14z. CIGs are expected to gradually lower with chances for MVFR increasing after 16-18z. Scattered showers are expected in the wake of the cold front Friday afternoon.
Southerly winds increase ahead of the front with gusts 25-30 kt along the coast. Inland will be a touch lower up to 20.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...High clouds continue to stream northward overhead with VFR conditions expected through at least 17-18z. Winds over the eastern metro have increased form the east to around 10 kt with gusts up to 20 kt. Expecting winds to decrease as the front approaches and the pressure gradient weakens. Light rain is expected after 12-14z as a front approaches the region. Chances for MVFR CIGs also increase to around 20-30% after 17z Fri as showers increase across the area. -19/DH

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: A 962 mb low spinning just south of the Gulf of Alaska will push an occluding front toward the coastal waters tonight. The surface low will gradually weaken as it drifts east, pushing up against the stalled frontal boundary over the outer waters. Southeast winds have already begun increasing this afternoon, and will continue to strengthen through tonight. The strongest winds are expected to persist across the outer coastal waters beyond 10 NM before the main front pushes across the waters late tonight into Friday morning. The Gale Warning remains in effect across the outer coastal waters from 4 PM this evening through 4 PM Friday, likely peaking between midnight and 6 AM with gusts up to 45 kt. There remains around a 30-50% chance for Storm Force wind gusts up to 50 kt, likely associated with the frontal passage. Breezy south winds are expected to persist through Friday afternoon before gradually diminishing Friday night.

Seas have subsided slightly to around 11 to 14 ft this afternoon as a westerly swell persists. The sea state becomes more complex later this evening into Friday as a dominant fresh swell out of the southwest moves into the waters. Seas become very steep and hazardous, gradually building back into the mid to upper teens with a dominant period of around 10-11 seconds by Friday afternoon. A strong, long period westerly swell then pushes into the waters later Friday afternoon which is expected to build seas above 20 ft by 3-4 PM. Significant wave heights are likely (60-80% chance) to build into the mid-20s Friday night before slowly subsiding on Saturday. Seas likely fall back into the upper teens by late Sat afternoon, but there is a 20% chance that seas remain at 20 ft or higher through Sat night as the next frontal system arrives.

Another deep low pressure system quickly spins up in the NE Pacific on Saturday pushing another strong front toward the coastal waters Sat night. Another round of strong southerly Gales is expected, while there is also a 50-70% chance for Storm Force wind gusts exceeding 50 kt across the outer coastal waters. Have issued a Storm Watch from 4 PM Sat to 4 AM Sunday. Another westerly swell will likely build seas above 20 ft again on Sunday with the swell persisting into Monday. /DH

sections.title: Beach hazards
paragraphs: A tidal anomaly from persistent southerly winds and warmer than average ocean temperatures will result in the total tide pushing 10.5 ft at the Garibaldi tidal gauge Friday afternoon. Historically this typically produces flooding along Fraser- Burton Road south of Tillamook along the Tillamook River. Elsewhere, lowland and agriculture flooding will occur, but it does not appear Highway 101 will be impacted in Pacific County where the Toke Point gauge is anticipated to top out near 11 ft.

More importantly, a large westerly swell will push towards the coast Friday afternoon and peak late Friday evening (most likely between 7-10 PM). This swell will take aim at the southern Oregon coast, but a swell of 25+ ft will still push onto the central and north Oregon coast while the swell will be closer to 20 ft along the south Washington coast. Given periods will be in the 17-19 second range, these waves will have a lot of mass and momentum than the typical Winter time storm swell. This will result in waves running significantly farther up on area beaches and jetties.

Or more simply put, the sneaker wave threat will be extreme. People should use extreme caution as sneaker waves can suddenly knock people off of their feet and quickly pull them into the frigid ocean which may lead to serious injury or drowning. In addition, large wave runup may dislodge logs on area beaches and result in them rolling up and down area beaches, which have historically killed or seriously injured unsuspecting people, so there will be much more of a threat than just getting wet from a rogue wave.

The large westerly swell will gradually subside Saturday. However, another westerly swell that will be pushing 20+ ft with dominant periods of 16-17 seconds arrives Sunday afternoon and lasts into Monday. This will necessitate another High Surf product and result in another round of high surf conditions, beach erosion and sneaker waves during this time. /Neuman
